claim: Rate-distortion theory provides a powerful framework for understanding the nature of human memory by formalizing the relationship between information rate and distortion.
source: Rate-distortion theory provides a powerful framework for understanding the nature of human memory by formalizing the relationship between information rate (the average number of bits per stimulus transmitted across the memory channel) and distortion (the cost of memory errors).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the applicability of rate-distortion theory to human memory, drawing on established mathematical framework.

claim: The population coding model reproduces key regularities of visual working memory.
source: The model reproduces key regularities of visual working memory, including some that were not previously explained by population coding models.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented throughout the manuscript comparing model predictions to empirical data.

claim: The model explains regularities that were not previously explained by population coding models.
source: The model reproduces key regularities of visual working memory, including some that were not previously explained by population coding models.
evidence: This is supported by the model's ability to explain serial dependence and timing effects, which are demonstrated in the results section.

claim: A novel prediction of the model is verified by reanalyzing recordings of monkey prefrontal neurons during an oculomotor delayed response task.
source: We verify a novel prediction of the model by reanalyzing recordings of monkey prefrontal neurons during an oculomotor delayed response task.
evidence: This is supported by the neural data analysis presented in Figure 8 showing the relationship between neural gain and memory error.

claim: All memory systems are capacity limited in the sense that a finite amount of information about the past can be stored and retrieved without error.
source: All memory systems are capacity limited in the sense that a finite amount of information about the past can be stored and retrieved without error.
evidence: This is a general principle based on established knowledge in cognitive science and information theory.

claim: Memory in the brain is error-prone, unlike most digital storage systems.
source: Most digital storage systems are designed to work without error. Memory in the brain, by contrast, is error-prone.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about biological versus digital memory systems.

claim: Working memory errors follow well-behaved functions of set size, variability, attention, among other factors.
source: In the domain of working memory, these errors follow well-behaved functions of set size, variability, attention, among other factors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and empirical regularities in the working memory literature.

claim: Memory regularities may emerge from maximization of memory performance subject to a capacity limit or encoding cost.
source: An important insight into the nature of such regularities was the recognition that they may emerge from maximization of memory performance subject to a capacity limit or encoding cost (Sims et al., 2012; Sims, 2015; van den Berg and Ma, 2018; Bates et al., 2019; Bates and Jacobs, 2020; Brady et al., 2009; Nassar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Rate-distortion theory provides a general formalization of the memory optimization problem.
source: Rate-distortion theory (Shannon, 1959) provides a general formalization of the memory optimization problem (reviewed in Sims, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shannon's foundational work and a review by Sims.

claim: Systems with higher capacity can achieve lower expected distortion, tracing out an optimal trade-off curve in the rate-distortion plane.
source: Systems with higher capacity can achieve lower expected distortion, tracing out an optimal trade-off curve in the rate-distortion plane.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of rate-distortion theory, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The hypothesis that human memory operates near the optimal trade-off curve allows one to deduce several known regularities of working memory errors.
source: The hypothesis that human memory operates near the optimal trade-off curve allows one to deduce several known regularities of working memory errors, some of which we describe below.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent demonstrations in the Results section showing model fits to empirical data.

claim: Past work has studied rate-distortion trade-offs in human memory.
source: Past work has studied rate-distortion trade-offs in human memory (Sims et al., 2012; Sims, 2015; Nagy et al., 2020), as well as in other domains such as category learning (Bates et al., 2019), perceptual identification (Sims, 2018), visual search (Bates and Jacobs, 2020), linguistic communication (Zaslavsky et al., 2018), and decision making (Gershman, 2020; Lai and Gershman, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Population coding offers a systematic account of working memory performance.
source: As exemplified by the work of Bays and his colleagues, population coding offers a systematic account of working memory performance (Bays, 2014; Bays, 2015; Bays, 2016; Schneegans and Bays, 2018; Schneegans et al., 2020; Taylor and Bays, 2018; Tomić and Bays, 2018), according to which errors arise from the readout of a noisy spiking population that encodes memoranda.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Bays and colleagues' work.

claim: A modified version of the population coding model implements the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm for rate-distortion optimization.
source: We show that a modified version of the population coding model implements the celebrated Blahut–Arimoto algorithm for rate-distortion optimization (Blahut, 1972; Arimoto, 1972).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the mathematical derivations in the Results section showing equivalence between the neural circuit equations and the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm.

claim: The modified population coding model can explain serial dependence.
source: The modified version can explain a number of phenomena that were puzzling under previous population coding accounts, such as serial dependence (the influence of previous trials on performance; Kiyonaga et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results in Figures 4-6 showing the model's ability to reproduce serial dependence effects.

claim: The Lagrange multiplier β controls the precision of the population code.
source: The Blahut–Arimoto algorithm is parametrized by a coefficient that specifies the trade-off between rate and distortion. In our circuit implementation, this coefficient controls the precision of the population code.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the mathematical formulation and illustrated in Figure 1C-E.

claim: A homeostatic learning rule adapts the coefficient β to maintain performance at the capacity limit.
source: We derive a homeostatic learning rule that adapts the coefficient to maintain performance at the capacity limit.
evidence: This is derived mathematically in Equation 14 and demonstrated through simulations.

claim: The homeostatic learning rule explains the dependence of memory performance on the intertrial and retention intervals.
source: This learning rule explains the dependence of memory performance on the intertrial and retention intervals (RIs) (Shipstead and Engle, 2013; Souza and Oberauer, 2015; Bliss et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results in Figure 3 matching empirical data from cited studies.

claim: The model predicts that performance should adapt across trials to maintain a set point close to the channel capacity.
source: It also makes the prediction that performance should adapt across trials to maintain a set point close to the channel capacity.
evidence: This prediction is tested and confirmed in the neural data analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Variations in performance track changes in neural gain.
source: Finally, we show that variations in performance track changes in neural gain, consistent with our theory.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8C showing correlation between fitted β and memory error.

claim: The optimal channel can be obtained by iterating Equations 4 and 5 until convergence, which is known as the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm.
source: One can obtain the optimal channel by initializing them to uniform distributions and iterating them until convergence. This is known as the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm (Blahut, 1972; Arimoto, 1972).
evidence: This is a standard algorithm from information theory, supported by citations.

claim: The firing rate of neuron i is determined by a Spike Response Model in which the membrane potential is the difference between excitatory input ui and inhibitory input b.
source: The firing rate of neuron i is determined by a simple Spike Response Model (Gerstner and Kistler, 2002) in which the membrane potential is the difference between the excitatory input, ui, and the inhibitory input, b, which we model as common across neurons
evidence: This is a model specification based on established neural modeling approaches, supported by citation.

claim: The resulting population dynamics is a form of 'winner-take-all' circuit.
source: The resulting population dynamics is a form of 'winner-take-all' circuit (Nessler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference about the circuit behavior, supported by citation.

claim: The spike-triggered learning rule is broadly in agreement with experimental studies.
source: This learning rule is broadly in agreement with experimental studies (Daoudal and Debanne, 2003; Cudmore and Turrigiano, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work on intrinsic plasticity.

claim: Channel capacity corresponds to a constraint on stimulus-driven deviations in firing rate from the marginal firing rate.
source: This expression reveals that channel capacity corresponds to a constraint on stimulus-driven deviations in firing rate from the marginal firing rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical expression for information rate in Equation 13.

claim: When the stimulus-driven firing rate is persistently greater than the marginal firing rate, the population may incur an unsustainably large metabolic cost.
source: When the stimulus-driven firing rate is persistently greater than the marginal firing rate, the population may incur an unsustainably large metabolic cost (Levy and Baxter, 1996; Laughlin et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to work on metabolic costs of neural activity.

claim: When the stimulus-driven firing rate is lower than the marginal firing rate, the population is underutilizing its information transmission resources.
source: When the stimulus-driven firing rate is lower than the marginal firing rate, the population is underutilizing its information transmission resources.
evidence: This is an inference from the rate-distortion framework.

claim: Adaptive gain modulation has been observed in neural circuits.
source: A similar adaptive gain modulation has been observed in neural circuits (Desai et al., 1999; Hengen et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work on homeostatic plasticity.

claim: Changes in background activity could mechanistically implement adaptive gain modulation.
source: Mechanistically, this could be implemented by changes in background activity: when stimulus-driven excitation is high, the inhibition will also be high (the network is balanced), and the ensuing noise will effectively decrease the gain (Chance et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic proposal supported by citation.

claim: The relationship between firing rate and extracellular calcium level is logarithmic.
source: More quantitatively, it has been posited that the relationship between firing rate and extracellular calcium level is logarithmic (King et al., 2001), consistent with the mathematical definition in Equation 13.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the model, capacity C corresponds to a calcium set point, and the gain parameter adapts to maintain this set point.
source: Thus, in this model, capacity C corresponds to a calcium set point, and the gain parameter adapts to maintain this set point.
evidence: This is an inference from the proposed calcium-based mechanism.

claim: A related mechanism has been proposed to control intrinsic excitability via calcium-driven changes in ion channel conductance.
source: A related mechanism has been proposed to control intrinsic excitability via calcium-driven changes in ion channel conductance (LeMasson et al., 1993; Abbott and LeMasson, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: When multiple stimuli are encoded, β will tend to be smaller because the same capacity constraint will be divided across more neurons.
source: As a consequence, β will tend to be smaller when more stimuli are encoded, because the same capacity constraint will be divided across more neurons.
evidence: This is an inference from the model equations for multiple stimuli.

claim: The persistence of the stimulus trace is determined by the gain parameter β.
source: Our model assumes that the excitatory input ui maintains a trace of the stimulus across the delay. The persistence of this trace is determined by the gain parameter β.
evidence: This is a model assumption and inference from the gain adaptation mechanism.

claim: The learning rule in Equation 14 will reduce β and thereby functionally decay the memory trace when persistently high levels of stimulus-evoked activity increase the information rate above the channel capacity.
source: Because persistently high levels of stimulus-evoked activity may, according to Equation 13, increase the information rate above the channel capacity, the learning rule in Equation 14 will reduce β and thereby functionally decay the memory trace.
evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics.

claim: Memory precision decreases with set size.
source: One of the most fundamental findings in the visual working memory literature is that memory precision decreases with set size (Bays et al., 2009; Bays, 2014; Wilken and Ma, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical work and is reproduced by the model in Figure 2.

claim: The model asserts that memory precision decreases with set size because the capacity constraint is divided across more neurons.
source: Our model asserts that this is the case because the capacity constraint of the system is divided across more neurons as the number of stimuli to be remembered increases, thus reducing the recall accuracy for any one stimulus.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that is supported by the model simulations in Figure 2.

claim: Error variance is reduced by a cue that probabilistically predicts the location of the probed stimulus.
source: For example, error variance is reduced by a cue that probabilistically predicts the location of the probed stimulus (Bays, 2014; Yoo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical work and is reproduced by the model in Figure 2.

claim: In the model, the cue is encoded by the probing probability πm, which alters the expected distortion and results in greater allocation of the capacity budget to cued stimuli.
source: In our model, the cue is encoded by the probing probability πm, which alters the expected distortion. This results in greater allocation of the capacity budget to cued stimuli than to uncued stimuli.
evidence: This is a model mechanism that is demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: Memory performance typically degrades with the retention interval.
source: It is well established that memory performance typically degrades with the RI (Pertzov et al., 2017; Panichello et al., 2019; Schneegans and Bays, 2018; Zhang and Luck, 2009), although the causes of this degradation are controversial (Oberauer et al., 2016), and in some cases the effect is unreliable (Shin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical work.

claim: According to the model, memory degradation with long retention intervals occurs because long RIs tax the information rate of the neural circuit.
source: According to our model, this occurs because long RIs tax the information rate of the neural circuit. In order to stay within the channel capacity, the circuit reduces the gain parameter β for long RIs, thereby reducing the information rate and degrading memory performance.
evidence: This is a model prediction that is demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: Longer intertrial intervals improve memory performance.
source: Memory performance also depends on the ITI, but in the opposite direction: longer ITIs improve performance (Souza and Oberauer, 2015; Shipstead and Engle, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical work and is reproduced by the model in Figure 3.

claim: The critical determinant of performance is the ratio between the ITI and RI.
source: The critical determinant of performance is in fact the ratio between the ITI and RI.
evidence: This is supported by the empirical findings from Souza and Oberauer, 2015 and the model simulations in Figure 3.

claim: Performance in a color working memory task was similar when both intervals were short or both intervals were long.
source: Souza and Oberauer, 2015 found that performance in a color working memory task was similar when both intervals were short or both intervals were long.
evidence: This is supported by citation to empirical work.

claim: A longer retention interval could produce better memory performance when it is paired with a longer intertrial interval.
source: They also reported that a longer RI could produce better memory performance when it is paired with a longer ITI.
evidence: This is supported by citation to empirical work from Souza and Oberauer, 2015.

claim: Timescale invariance arises as a direct consequence of Equation 16.
source: This timescale invariance, which is also seen in studies of associative learning (Balsam and Gallistel, 2009), arises as a direct consequence of Equation 16.
evidence: This is an inference from the mathematical model, with additional citation to related work.

claim: Working memory recall is biased by recent stimuli, a phenomenon known as serial dependence.
source: Working memory recall is biased by recent stimuli, a phenomenon known as serial dependence (Fischer and Whitney, 2014; Fritsche et al., 2017; Bliss et al., 2017; Papadimitriou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical work.

claim: Recall is generally attracted toward recent stimuli.
source: Recall is generally attracted toward recent stimuli, though some studies have reported repulsive effects when the most recent and current stimulus differ by a large amount (Barbosa et al., 2020; Bliss et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical work.

claim: The theory explains serial dependence as a consequence of the marginal firing rate of the output cells, which biases the excitatory input.
source: Our theory explains serial dependence as a consequence of the marginal firing rate of the output cells, which biases the excitatory input ui (see Equation 10).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the model mechanism.

claim: The marginal firing rate reflects recent stimulus history because it is updated incrementally.
source: Because the marginal firing rate is updated incrementally, it will reflect recent stimulus history.
evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics.

claim: Serial dependence increases with the retention interval and decreases with intertrial interval.
source: An important benchmark for theories of serial dependence is the finding that it increases with the RI and decreases with ITI (Bliss et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to empirical work and is reproduced by the model in Figure 4.

claim: The strength of serial dependence varies inversely with the information rate.
source: Our explanation of serial dependence is closely related to our explanation of timing effects on recall error: the strength of serial dependence varies inversely with the information rate, which in turn increases with the ITI and decreases with the RI.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that is demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: Serial dependence has been shown to build up over the course of an experimental session.
source: Serial dependence has also been shown to build up over the course of an experimental session (Barbosa and Compte, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to empirical work and is reproduced by the model in Figure 5.

claim: The bias induced by the marginal firing rate integrates over the entire stimulus history, thereby building up over the course of an experimental session.
source: Because this bias reflects continuous incremental adjustments, it integrates over the entire stimulus history, thereby building up over the course of an experimental session (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference from the model mechanism, demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: If serial dependence reflects a capacity limit, then it should increase with set size.
source: If, as we hypothesize, serial dependence reflects a capacity limit, then we should expect it to increase with set size, since β must decrease to stay within the capacity limit.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is tested empirically.

claim: The attractive bias for similar stimuli on consecutive trials is stronger when the set size is larger.
source: Figure 6 shows that the attractive bias for similar stimuli on consecutive trials is stronger when the set size is larger (p < 0.05, group permutation test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Panichello et al., 2019, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Working memory exhibits systematic biases toward stimuli that are shown more frequently than others.
source: Working memory exhibits systematic biases toward stimuli that are shown more frequently than others (Panichello et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to empirical work and is reproduced by the model in Figure 7.

claim: Systematic biases increase with the retention interval and build up over the course of an experimental session.
source: Moreover, these biases increase with the RI, and build up over the course of an experimental session.
evidence: This is supported by the empirical data and model simulations in Figure 7.

claim: Over the course of the experiment, the marginal firing rate asymptotically approaches the distribution of presented stimuli.
source: Our theory posits that, over the course of the experiment, the marginal firing rate asymptotically approaches the distribution of presented stimuli (assuming there are no inhomogeneities in the distortion function).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the model.

claim: Neurons corresponding to high-frequency stimuli become more excitable than others and bias recall toward their preferred stimuli.
source: Thus, the neurons corresponding to high-frequency stimuli become more excitable than others and bias recall toward their preferred stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference from the model mechanism, demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: The bias toward high-frequency stimuli is amplified by lower effective capacities brought about by longer retention intervals.
source: This bias is amplified by lower effective capacities brought about by longer RIs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: The full rate-distortion model has an average protected exceedance probability of 0.76 across datasets.
source: All the other datasets provided moderate to strong evidence in favor of the full rate-distortion model, with an average protected exceedance probability of 0.76.
evidence: This is based on Bayesian model comparison results presented in Table 1.

claim: Operating below the channel capacity will lead to an increase in the gain term β, which leads to a higher information rate and better memory performance.
source: Equation 14 predicts that operating below the channel capacity will lead to an increase in the gain term β, which, in turn, leads to a higher information rate and better memory performance.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model equation.

claim: The model predicts that recall accuracy should improve after a period of poor memory performance, and degrade after a period of good memory performance.
source: Therefore, our model predicts that recall accuracy should improve after a period of poor memory performance, and degrade after a period of good memory performance.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is tested in Figure 8A.

claim: The model predicts that error will tend to be lower when gain (β) is higher.
source: At the neural level, the model predicts that error will tend to be lower when gain (β) is higher.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is tested in Figure 8C.

claim: Squared error was significantly lower following higher-than-average error than following lower-than-average error.
source: Behavioraly, squared error was significantly lower following higher-than-average error than following lower-than-average error (linear mixed model, p < 0.001; Figure 8A), consistent with the hypothesis that gain tends to increase after poor performance and decrease after good performance.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of monkey behavioral data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Session-specific mean squared error was negatively correlated with the average β estimate.
source: We then examined the relationship between neural gain and memory precision across sessions, finding that session-specific mean squared error was negatively correlated with the average β estimate (r = –0.32, p < 0.02; Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of neural data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Dynamic changes in memory performance are associated with changes in neural gain.
source: This result is consistent with the hypothesis that dynamic changes in memory performance are associated with changes in neural gain.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis in Figure 8C.

claim: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is a region classically associated with maintenance of information in working memory.
source: The neural data were collected from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a region classically associated with maintenance of information in working memory (Levy and Goldman-Rakic, 2000; Funahashi, 2006; Wimmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The hypothesis that neural systems are designed to optimize a rate-distortion trade-off has been previously studied through the lens of the information bottleneck method.
source: The hypothesis that neural systems are designed to optimize a rate-distortion trade-off has been previously studied through the lens of the information bottleneck method (Bialek et al., 2006; Klampfl et al., 2009; Buesing and Maass, 2010; Palmer et al., 2015), a special case of rate-distortion theory in which the distortion function is derived from a compression principle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Minimizing the rate-distortion objective using alternating optimization is not guaranteed to find the globally optimal channel when using the information bottleneck method.
source: One consequence of this dependency is that minimizing the rate-distortion objective using alternating optimization (in the style of the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm) is not guaranteed to find the globally optimal channel.
evidence: This is an inference from the mathematical properties of the information bottleneck method.

claim: Existing spiking neuron implementations of the information bottleneck method do not attain the same level of generality as the approach using a reference distribution.
source: However, existing spiking neuron implementations of the information bottleneck method (Klampfl et al., 2009; Buesing and Maass, 2010) do not make use of such a reference distribution, and hence do not attain the same level of generality.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and comparison with the reference distribution approach.

claim: Leibfried and Braun, 2015 propose a spiking neuron model that explicitly optimizes the rate-distortion objective function for arbitrary distortion functions.
source: Leibfried and Braun, 2015 propose a spiking neuron model that explicitly optimizes the rate-distortion objective function for arbitrary distortion functions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Leibfried and Braun's approach differs from the current model in that they model a single neuron rather than a population.
source: Their approach differs from ours in several ways. First, they model a single neuron, rather than a population.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited prior work.

claim: Leibfried and Braun posit that the channel optimization is realized through synaptic plasticity, in contrast to the intrinsic plasticity rule studied in the current model.
source: Second, they posit that the channel optimization is realized through synaptic plasticity, in contrast to the intrinsic plasticity rule that we study here.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited prior work.

claim: Leibfried and Braun treat the gain parameter β as fixed, whereas the current model proposes an algorithm for optimizing β.
source: Third, they treat the gain parameter β as fixed, whereas we propose an algorithm for optimizing β.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited prior work.

claim: Spiking activity accounts for a large fraction of cortical energy expenditure.
source: Spiking activity accounts for a large fraction of cortical energy expenditure (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Lennie, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A limit on the overall firing rate of a neural population is a natural transmission bottleneck.
source: Thus, a limit on the overall firing rate of a neural population is a natural transmission bottleneck.
evidence: This is an inference from the metabolic cost of spiking.

claim: Previous work on energy-efficient coding has used the cost of spiking as a constraint.
source: Previous work on energy-efficient coding has similarly used the cost of spiking as a constraint (Levy and Baxter, 1996; Stemmler and Koch, 1999; Balasubramanian et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Firing rate tends to be maintained around a set point rather than minimized.
source: This means that the average firing rate can be high provided the stimulus-evoked transients are small, consistent with the observation that firing rate tends to be maintained around a set point rather than minimized (Desai et al., 1999; Hengen et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The set point should correspond to the capacity limit.
source: The set point should correspond to the capacity limit.
evidence: This is an inference from the model framework.

claim: At the single neuron level, gain control might be realized by adaptation of voltage conductances.
source: At the single neuron level, this might be realized by adaptation of voltage conductances (Stemmler and Koch, 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic proposal supported by citation.

claim: At the population level, neuromodulators could act as a global gain control.
source: At the population level, neuromodulators could act as a global gain control.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic proposal.

claim: Catecholamines have been thought to play a role in global gain control.
source: Catecholamines (e.g., dopamine and norepinephrine), in particular, have been thought to play this role (Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990; Durstewitz et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Local injection of dopamine D1 receptor antagonists into the prefrontal cortex impaired performance in an oculomotor delayed response task.
source: Directly relevant to this hypothesis are experiments showing that local injection of dopamine D1 receptor antagonists into the prefrontal cortex impaired performance in an oculomotor delayed response task (Sawaguchi and Goldman-Rakic, 1991), whereas D1 agonists can improve performance (Castner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Dopamine D1 agonists can improve performance in delayed response tasks.
source: Directly relevant to this hypothesis are experiments showing that local injection of dopamine D1 receptor antagonists into the prefrontal cortex impaired performance in an oculomotor delayed response task (Sawaguchi and Goldman-Rakic, 1991), whereas D1 agonists can improve performance (Castner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Pharmacological manipulations of dopamine can have non-monotonic effects on cognitive performance, with the direction of the effect depending on baseline dopamine levels.
source: In experiments with humans, it has been reported that pharmacological manipulations of dopamine can have non-monotonic effects on cognitive performance, with the direction of the effect depending on baseline dopamine levels (see Cools and D'Esposito, 2011 for a review).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Baseline dopamine level (particularly in the striatum) correlates with working memory performance.
source: The baseline level (particularly in the striatum) correlates with working memory performance (Cools et al., 2008; Landau et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical work.

claim: Dopaminergic neuromodulation controls the capacity limit, possibly through a gain control mechanism.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that dopaminergic neuromodulation controls the capacity limit (possibly through a gain control mechanism), and that pushing dopamine levels beyond the system's capacity provokes a compensatory decrease in gain, as predicted by our homeostatic model of gain adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited empirical findings and the model predictions.

claim: Pushing dopamine levels beyond the system's capacity provokes a compensatory decrease in gain.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that dopaminergic neuromodulation controls the capacity limit (possibly through a gain control mechanism), and that pushing dopamine levels beyond the system's capacity provokes a compensatory decrease in gain, as predicted by our homeostatic model of gain adaptation.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is consistent with cited empirical findings.

claim: With appropriate modification, the rate-distortion framework can be applied more broadly to tasks like serial order, AX-CPT, and N-back tasks.
source: For example, serial order, AX-CPT, and N-back tasks are widely used but outside the scope of our model. With appropriate modification, the rate-distortion framework can be applied more broadly.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future extensions of the model.

claim: One could construct channels for sequences rather than individual items, analogous to how the model handles multiple simultaneously presented stimuli.
source: For example, one could construct channels for sequences rather than individual items, analogous to how we have handled multiple simultaneously presented stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for model extension.

claim: Previous work has suggested that working memory representations are efficient codes that encode some stimuli with higher precision than others.
source: Previous work has suggested that working memory representations are efficient codes that encode some stimuli with higher precision than others (Koyluoglu et al., 2017; Taylor and Bays, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recent applications of large-scale neural networks, such as the variational autoencoder, to modeling human memory hold promise.
source: Recent applications of large-scale neural networks, such as the variational autoencoder, to modeling human memory hold promise (Nagy et al., 2020; Bates and Jacobs, 2020; Franklin et al., 2020; Bates et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023), though linking these to more realistic neural circuits remains a challenge.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work, with acknowledgment of remaining challenges.

claim: Model comparison using the Bayesian information criterion established that both the distortion function and spiking history were significant predictors of spiking behavior.
source: Model comparison using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) established that both the distortion function (which captures driving input) and spiking history were significant predictors of spiking behavior (full model: 54,545; no history: 59,163; neither distortion nor history: 67,903).
evidence: This is supported by BIC values from model comparison on neural data.

claim: When only a single stimulus is presented (M=1), the gain is high and the output neurons report the true stimulus with high precision.
source: When only a single stimulus is presented (M=1), the gain is high and the output neurons report the true stimulus with high precision.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1D showing narrow spike distribution.

claim: When multiple stimuli are presented (M=4), the gain is lower and the output has reduced precision.
source: When multiple stimuli are presented (M=4), the gain is lower and the output has reduced precision (i.e., sometimes the wrong output neuron fires).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1E showing broader spike distribution.

claim: For every point on the rate-distortion curve, the same information rate achieves a lower distortion for set size 1 compared to set size 4.
source: For every point on the curve, the same information rate achieves a lower distortion for set size 1, due to the fact that all of the channel capacity can be devoted to a single stimulus (a hypothetical capacity limit is shown by the dashed horizontal line).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C comparing rate-distortion curves for different set sizes.
